text: BMJ umbrella review: largest all-cause mortality risk reduction (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.83-0.88) at 3-4 cups/day vs none.
quote: largest relative risk reduction at intakes of three to four cups a day versus none, including all cause mortality (relative risk 0.83, 95% confidence interval 0.83 to 0.88), cardiovascular mortality (0.81, 0.72 to 0.90), and cardiovascular disease (0.85, 0.80 to 0.90)

text: BMJ umbrella review: high vs low coffee consumption associated with 30% lower type 2 diabetes risk (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.65-0.75).
quote: Coffee consumption was consistently associated with a lower risk of type 2 diabetes for high versus low consumption (relative risk 0.70, 95% confidence interval 0.65 to 0.75)

text: BMJ umbrella review concludes RCTs are still needed to establish whether coffee's associations with health outcomes are causal.
quote: Robust randomised controlled trials are needed to understand whether the observed associations are causal.

text: Umbrella review graded evidence quality: about 25% of outcomes 'low' and 75% 'very low' by GRADE.
quote: about 25% were rated as being of “low” and 75% as “very low” quality with the GRADE classification

text: Authors note Mendelian randomisation studies found no genetic evidence of a causal link for T2D or mortality, suggesting residual confounding.
quote: The association between coffee consumption and lower risk of type 2 diabetes122 and all cause and cardiovascular mortality123 was found to have no genetic evidence for a causal relation in Mendelian randomisation studies, suggesting residual confounding could result in the observed associations in other studies.

text: Benefit plateaus rather than reverses above 3-4 cups/day; no increased harm at higher intake, just smaller benefit.
quote: Increasing consumption to above three cups a day was not associated with harm, but the beneficial effect was less pronounced

text: Danish MR study: observational U-shaped mortality/CVD benefit was NOT replicated by genetic (caffeine-allele) analysis.
quote: Observationally, coffee intake was associated with U-shaped lower risk of cardiovascular disease and all-cause mortality; however, genetically caffeine intake was not associated with risk of cardiovascular disease or all-cause mortality.

text: Observationally, lowest risk of IHD, ischaemic stroke, IVD and all-cause mortality occurred at medium coffee intake (U-shape).
quote: we observed U-shaped associations with extent of coffee intake for IHD, IS, IVD and all-cause mortality with lowest risks for individuals with medium coffee intake compared with individuals with no coffee intake

text: Genetic caffeine-allele hazard ratios were close to 1 (null) for all five cardiometabolic/mortality endpoints tested.
quote: Hazard ratios per caffeine intake allele were 1.02 (95% confidence interval: 1.00–1.03) for ischaemic heart disease, 1.02 (0.99–1.02) for ischaemic stroke, 1.02 (1.00–1.03) for ischaemic vascular disease, 1.02 (0.99–1.06) for cardiovascular mortality and 1.01 (0.99–1.03) for all-cause mortality.

text: Study's genetic instrument had 80% power to detect only a small causal effect, smaller than the observed association.
quote: we could exclude odds ratio per allele of 0.97 for 8% higher coffee intake with 80% power

text: Authors interpret the null genetic result as evidence the observational benefit is likely confounded, not causal.
quote: we believe that our genetic results also suggest confounding as possible explanations for the previously observed ‘beneficial’ associations with moderate coffee intake, and thus that coffee intake is unlikely to influence risk of CVD or all-cause mortality.

text: Danish MR study: observational T2D/obesity/metabolic-syndrome benefit found no supporting genetic evidence of causality.
quote: High coffee intake was associated observationally with low risk of obesity, metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes, and was associated observationally with related components thereof, but with no genetic evidence to support corresponding causal relationships.

text: Coffee-intake genetic risk score: 9-10 vs 0-3 alleles corresponded to 29% higher actual coffee intake.
quote: 9-10 vs 0-3 coffee-intake alleles were associated with 29% higher coffee intake

text: Per-allele meta-analysed odds ratios for type 2 diabetes clustered near 1.0 (null) across genetic variants.
quote: Per-allele meta-analysed odds ratios for type 2 diabetes were 1.01 (0.98-1.04) for AHR rs4410790, 0.98 (0.95-1.01) for AHR rs6968865, 1.01 (0.99-1.03) for CYP1A1/2 rs2470893

text: Observationally, high coffee intake was linked to higher BMI, blood pressure, triglycerides and cholesterol, not lower glucose.
quote: high coffee intake was associated with high body mass index, waist circumference, weight, height, systolic/diastolic blood pressure, triglycerides and total cholesterol and with low high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, but not with glucose levels

text: Study population: 93,179 individuals from two large general-population cohorts.
quote: We included 93,179 individuals from two large general population cohorts in a Mendelian randomization study.
